findings.claim_source_sentence: Public untargeted metabolomics data is a growing resource for metabolite and phenotype discovery; however, accessing and utilizing these data across repositories pose significant challenges.
findings.evidence: Develops pan-repository identifiers and harmonized metadata to enable cross-repository reanalysis.
findings.study_system: public metabolomics repositories (MetaboLights, Metabolomics Workbench, GNPS/MassIVE)

findings.claim: MetaboLights is a cross-species, cross-technique global metabolomics repository holding raw data and associated metadata, recommended by leading journals and ELIXIR, with community reuse of public data.
findings.claim_source_sentence: MetaboLights is a global database for metabolomics studies including the raw experimental data and the associated metadata.
findings.evidence: Repository description covering standardized workflows (MetaboLights Labs) and documented reuse of public data.
findings.study_system: MetaboLights metabolomics repository

findings.claim: Raw data in major metabolomics repositories lack standardization of file/system formats, making it difficult for non-experts to reuse deposited datasets in downstream analysis platforms; CloMet converts MetaboLights/Metabolomics Workbench data into analysis-ready formats.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Yet, the raw data stored in the aforementioned repositories lack standardization in terms of the file system format used to store the associated acquisition files.
findings.evidence: Open-source converter bridging repositories and analysis platforms to improve reusability and reproducibility.
findings.study_system: metabolomics repositories (MetaboLights, Metabolomics Workbench) and analysis platforms

findings.claim: The HHEAR public data repository harmonizes environmental-exposure biomarker and epidemiologic data across studies using a common ontology and knowledge graph, aligning to FAIR principles, and will eventually contain data from tens of thousands of individuals across dozens of studies.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The latest semantic technologies are used to efficiently conduct data standardization across studies and promote data sharing by aligning the repository with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles.
findings.evidence: FAIR-aligned exposomics repository using semantic standardization to a common ontology.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The repository will eventually contain information from 35,989 individuals across 55 environmental health studies, including data on biomarkers of environmental exposures, sociodemographics, health outcomes, and physical and mental assessments.
findings.study_system: HHEAR environmental epidemiology data repository

findings.claim: SSBD was restructured into a two-tiered resource (a broad repository plus a curated metadata-rich database) to reconcile the conflicting demands of rapid data publication and richly annotated, highly reusable bioimaging data.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This update addresses the conflicting demands of rapid data publication and sharing of richly annotated data, thereby promoting bioimaging data sharing and reuse.
findings.evidence: Bioimaging data ecosystem balancing rapid sharing against curated reusability, with metadata harmonization for cross-resource exchange.
findings.study_system: SSBD bioimaging data repository/database

findings.claim: Sharing and standardizing biomedical imaging data across modalities remains a global challenge, driving international efforts to build FAIR, interoperable frameworks bridging biological and clinical imaging communities.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This article examines the global challenges and emerging solutions in sharing and standardizing biomedical imaging data across modalities.
findings.evidence: Perspective on consensus-building and infrastructure for global imaging data interoperability.
findings.study_system: biomedical imaging data-sharing standards

findings.claim: High-content screening generates massive heterogeneous metadata (images, reagents, protocols, analytics, phenotypes) that must be linked and shared, posing a unique data-management challenge addressed via OMERO-based workflow management systems.
findings.claim_source_sentence: However, it generates massive amounts of metadata, making HCS experiments a unique data management challenge.
findings.evidence: Reusable semi-automatic workflows for FAIR image data management on OMERO.
findings.study_system: high-content screening bioimaging data management (OMERO)

findings.claim: A rule-based completeness assessment of a large single-center EHR found substantial missingness across vocabulary fields, observations, and other tables, illustrating that real-world clinical data often falls short of research-fitness on completeness dimensions.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The rule-based assessment identified substantial missingness in vocabulary fields (38/124, 30.6%) and missing or special characteristic values in relation to observations (3,643,581/15,313,287, 23.8%), measurements (25,583,622/642,623,715, 4%), care sites (28/1715, 1.6%), and deaths (117/34,330, 0.3%).
findings.evidence: Multi-perspective completeness assessment (structural, rule-based, descriptive) of an EHR dataset for research.
findings.effect_size: 30.6% of vocabulary fields and 23.8% of observations with missing/special values
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The rule-based assessment identified substantial missingness in vocabulary fields (38/124, 30.6%) and missing or special characteristic values in relation to observations (3,643,581/15,313,287, 23.8%), measurements (25,583,622/642,623,715, 4%), care sites (28/1715, 1.6%), and deaths (117/34,330, 0.3%).
findings.study_system: single-center Korean EHR dataset (OMOP-structured)

findings.claim: Mapping lung cancer data to the OMOP Common Data Model achieved high consistency for structured variables but excluded free-text variables and was hampered by evolving data-dictionary versions and cross-institution granularity mismatches.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Persistent issues included evolving data dictionary versions and mismatches in diagnostic code granularity between institutions, underscoring structural challenges in standardization.
findings.evidence: Observational evaluation of OMOP CDM mapping quality (consistency via Cohen kappa; completeness via counts).
findings.study_system: OMOP CDM mapping of lung cancer EHR data (Ghent University Hospital)

findings.claim: In a single-institution study, biomarker data present in the source EHR were lost in the vast majority of downstream FHIR extracts, revealing severe fidelity gaps when real-world oncology data are exchanged between systems.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In contrast, biomarker data present in the source EHR were missing in 80%-100% of FHIR extracts.
findings.evidence: Retrospective concordance study comparing source EHR, cancer registry, and FHIR exports against manual chart review.
findings.effect_size: 80%-100% of FHIR extracts missing source-EHR biomarker data
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In contrast, biomarker data present in the source EHR were missing in 80%-100% of FHIR extracts.
findings.study_system: lung cancer real-world data (EHR/registry/FHIR)

findings.claim: Even with LOINC as a semantic-interoperability standard, 6-19% of laboratory tests cannot be accurately mapped; a system-agnostic remediation framework raised unit conformance from ~73% to ~99.7% across billions of oncology lab records.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Studies show that 6% to 19% of laboratory tests cannot be accurately mapped to LOINC.
findings.evidence: Framework correcting LOINC code-unit conformance across a ~10 million-patient oncology database.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Before applying the framework, 73.1% (4,634,610,173/6,337,101,453) of records in the ConcertAI dataset had correctly assigned units based on the laboratory reasonable range table; after application, this increased to 99.7% (6,322,375,200/6,341,230,213).
findings.study_system: multi-source oncology real-world lab data (ConcertAI)

findings.claim: A quantitative comparison of five major biomedical terminology systems found SNOMED CT had superior granularity in most clinical domains, and introduced metrics for the semantic degradation that occurs when translating between vocabularies.
findings.claim_source_sentence: SNOMED CT exhibited superior granularity across most clinical domains, with some exceptions (ICD-10-CM in "Qualifier value," GO in "Observable entity," and LOINC in "Staging and scales.")
findings.evidence: Novel metrics (structural size, mapping burden ratio, content overlap) quantifying semantic integration potential via UMLS Metathesaurus.
findings.study_system: SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD-10-CM, Gene Ontology, CPT

findings.claim: Conflicting disease coding systems constrain interoperability; the Mondo disease ontology was built as a community-driven system harmonizing OMIM, Orphanet, MeSH, NCIt and others into one computable framework with provenanced links back to sources.
findings.claim_source_sentence: To address these issues, we created the Mondo disease ontology-a community-driven, open-source, unified disease classification system that harmonizes diverse terminologies into a consistent, computable framework.
findings.evidence: Ontology integrating multiple disease terminologies with attributed cross-references.
findings.study_system: Mondo disease ontology

findings.claim: The Ontology of Adverse Events grew to 10,829 formally defined terms, adding 7,741 new terms since 2014, reflecting substantial expansion of clinical granularity for standardizing adverse-event data.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Current statistical analysis reveals that OAE has 10,829 formally defined terms with unique identifiers.
findings.evidence: Documented ontology extension for structured, cross-disciplinary adverse-event representation.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Compared to the 3,088 ontology terms included in the last OAE publication in 2014, 7,741 new terms have been added to OAE, which represents significant progress of the ontology in clinical granularity and domain coverage.
findings.study_system: Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE)

findings.claim: A BioAssay Ontology update to improve coverage of PK/PD and safety-pharmacology assays was driven by an industry electronic-lab-notebook data initiative (Pistoia Alliance), improving semantic precision, external-ontology alignment, and reasoning.
findings.claim_source_sentence: These refinements, driven by collaboration with the Semantic Enrichment of Electronic Laboratory Notebook Data project, an industry initiative led by the Pistoia Alliance, address previously identified gaps in ontology coverage.
findings.evidence: Ontology extension linking ELN metadata capture to standardized assay representation.
findings.study_system: BioAssay Ontology (BAO v2.8.16)

findings.claim: Existing electronic lab notebooks often lack cross-platform interoperability, authorship certification, and immutable auditability; IntegriLAB adds blockchain-based cryptographic certification of research activities to strengthen reproducibility.
findings.claim_source_sentence: While current Electronic Lab Notebooks (ELNs) aid organization, they often lack cross-platform interoperability, authorship certification, and immutable auditability.
findings.evidence: Proof-of-concept ELN integrating DataLad/Overleaf/GitHub with blockchain verification.
findings.study_system: electronic lab notebook for neuroimaging (IntegriLAB)

findings.claim: The technical complexity of neuroimaging workflows makes them hard to document reproducibly; QuNex recipes capture every processing step and parameter so a study can be replicated from only the software version, recipe file, and data.
findings.claim_source_sentence: These complexities make it difficult to document workflows in sufficient detail to ensure complete transparency and reproducibility.
findings.evidence: Human- and machine-readable executable workflow specification for reproducible neuroimaging.
findings.study_system: neuroimaging workflow provenance (QuNex recipes)

findings.claim: Few empirical studies examine which governance policies biobanks actually implement; interviews across four Japanese biobanks surfaced an inherent tension between scientific advancement and ethical practice that shaped everyday governance.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Despite this importance, only a limited number of empirical studies have examined which governance policies are actually implemented in biobank operations and what challenges arise in practice.
findings.evidence: Qualitative interview study of biobank governance in practice.
findings.study_system: Japanese biobanks (governance)

findings.claim: A systematic review of genomic data-sharing willingness found trust, not factual genomic literacy, was the central determinant, often compensating for limited literacy, while financial considerations played only a minor role.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Trust was a central factor influencing willingness to share data, often compensating for limited genomic literacy.
findings.evidence: PRISMA systematic review of 15 empirical studies (2015-2025) on genomic data sharing and health literacy.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria.
findings.study_system: systematic review: patient genomic data-sharing willingness

findings.claim: Commercial genomics companies increasingly perform core biobanking functions and treat genomic data/biospecimens as saleable corporate assets, exposing governance gaps when firms are restructured, acquired, or become insolvent.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Contemporary genomics companies increasingly perform core biobanking functions-collecting, storing, and sharing large volumes of genetic data and biospecimens-without being widely recognized or governed as biobanks.
findings.evidence: Comparative case study (Nigerian genomics firm, DNA marketplaces, 23andMe sale) of genomic assetization governance.
findings.study_system: commercial genomics biobanking governance

findings.claim: In a 527-participant simulation, altruism and perceived benefit drove willingness to share medical data with researchers while privacy concerns and patient activation reduced it, and demographic factors were not significant predictors.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Altruism and perceived benefit drive willingness to share health data, while privacy concerns and patient activation may reduce it, emphasizing the need for patient-centered, transparent consent models.
findings.evidence: Mixed-methods simulation study (iAgree platform) with logistic regression and thematic analysis.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We conducted a mixed-methods study with 527 US adults (≥18 years) recruited via advisory boards, social media, clinics, and newsletters.
findings.study_system: US adults, medical data-sharing consent simulation

findings.claim: A systematic review of Australian genomic data governance found the prevailing reliance on individual consent as the primary protection mechanism, plus divergent clinical vs research priorities, must be addressed before a national framework can advance.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Our synthesis of the current literature on genomic data governance suggests that the current focus on individual consent as the primary mechanism for protecting data subjects and different priorities in clinical and research governance need to be addressed.
findings.evidence: Systematic review (Scopus, PubMed) of 31 articles via inductive content analysis.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Thirty-one relevant articles were included and were analysed using inductive content analysis.
findings.study_system: systematic review: Australian genomic data governance

findings.claim: In a national survey on Korea's bio-big-data project, willingness to participate was driven more by personal benefit than public interest, and respondents preferred dynamic consent over broad consent.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Willingness to participate varied by incentive: 60.9% expressed willingness to participate when personal benefits were offered, 29.9% were motivated by public interest, and 9.3% declined participation altogether.
findings.evidence: Web/mobile survey of 1,027 Korean adults on consent models, governance, and participation drivers.
findings.effect_size: 60.9% willing with personal benefit vs 29.9% for public interest
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Willingness to participate varied by incentive: 60.9% expressed willingness to participate when personal benefits were offered, 29.9% were motivated by public interest, and 9.3% declined participation altogether.
findings.study_system: Korean adults, national bio-big-data participation survey

findings.claim: Most electronic data capture/management systems use generic entity-attribute-value schemas that enable flexible study deployment but are cumbersome to query, especially across multiple systems; CohortExplorer provides a generic API abstracting EAV metadata (demonstrated on REDCap and Opal).
findings.claim_source_sentence: Most electronic data capture (EDC) and electronic data management (EDM) systems developed to collect and store clinical data from participants recruited into studies are based on generic entity-attribute-value (EAV) database schemas which enable rapid and flexible deployment in a range of study designs.
findings.evidence: Generic query API over EAV/CDISC ODM metadata, plug-and-play with REDCap and Opal.
findings.study_system: clinical EDC systems (REDCap, Opal) EAV schemas

findings.claim: Inconsistent metadata forces researchers to spend over 40% of curation time on manual standardization; a fine-tuned language-model harmonizer reached 96% in-dictionary accuracy but only 17% for previously unseen standard terms.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This fragmentation forces researchers to spend over 40% of curation time on manual standardization.
findings.evidence: GPT-2 fine-tuning with data augmentation to map researcher-specific metadata to standard vocabulary terms across domains.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Fine-tuned models achieve 96% in-dictionary accuracy, reducing manual effort by over 90% when the term exists in the vocabulary, and 17% out-of-dictionary accuracy for previously unseen standards, outperforming traditional heuristics and zero-shot GPT-4o.
findings.study_system: biomedical metadata harmonization (language models)

findings.claim: Structured Data Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) templates markedly improved completeness of NIH-required elements versus unstructured plans, yet about one-fifth of submitted DMSPs still omitted at least one required element.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We evaluated the content of the 358 DMSPs using the rubric developed for this study (Supplementary Material); 79.3% of them addressed all six required elements outlined in the NIH DMS Policy.
findings.evidence: 18-month audit of NIH grant DMSPs at one academic medical center, scored with a compliance rubric; structured local/NIH templates versus unstructured idiosyncratic plans.
findings.effect_size: 79.3% addressed all six required elements; sub-element completeness ranged 98.9% to 49.3%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Similarly, the percent of sub-elements addressed varied from 98.9% for data type description to 49.3% for data generation process description (Table).
findings.study_system: NIH grant Data Management and Sharing Plans, single academic medical center

findings.claim: Only a quarter of high-impact rehabilitation studies included a data-sharing statement, and when authors who declared data 'available on request' were contacted, follow-through was low.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Of the 1,278 studies that underwent data extraction, 326 (25.51%) contained DSS.
findings.evidence: Cross-sectional PRISMA-style audit of 1,278 clinical studies in five top rehabilitation journals (2017-2023), plus email requests to corresponding authors to test willingness to share.
findings.effect_size: 326/1278 (25.51%) contained a data-sharing statement; of 89 responding authors, 43 (48.31%) willing to share unconditionally
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We sent 251 emails to the corresponding authors and received 89 (35.46%) responses within two weeks. Of the 89 respondents, 43 (48.31%) were willing to share de-identified data unconditionally, while 16 (17.98%) were willing to share it only under specific conditions.
findings.study_system: high-impact rehabilitation journal clinical studies, 2017-2023

findings.claim: Coordinated community curation replaced roughly 220 million project-specific variant IDs with standard reference SNP identifiers (rsIDs) to make agricultural genetic-variation data interoperable and reusable, closing a gap where agricultural genomics has lagged human genomics in FAIR practices.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In total, nearly or almost 220 million custom variant IDs were replaced with stable rsIDs: 78.9 million in maize, 67.7 million in rice, 46.4 million in sorghum, 26.3 million in Arabidopsis, and 315,353 in grapevine.
findings.evidence: AgBioData working-group effort brokering submissions to the European Variation Archive and adopting rsIDs across crop pangenome/community databases.
findings.effect_size: ~220 million custom IDs replaced with rsIDs; sorghum community rsIDs rose from 8 million to over 55 million
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In sorghum, the submission of three major studies increased the number of rsIDs available to the community from 8 million in EVA release 3 (February 2022) to over 55 million in release 7 (April 2025).
findings.study_system: agricultural genomics (crops/livestock), European Variation Archive

findings.claim: ClarID embeds core biological metadata (project, species, tissue, disease, assay) into human-readable, machine-parsable identifiers to reduce reliance on detached metadata files, and was demonstrated at scale on Genomic Data Commons records.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We focused on ‘clinical.tsv’, which contained 210 columns and 113,760 rows across 86 studies (including 33 from TCGA).
findings.evidence: Identifier specification (YAML codebook + open-source ClarID-Tools CLI) applied to GDC clinical and biospecimen tables to generate interpretable subject/biosample IDs.
findings.effect_size: 113,760 clinical (subject) records across 86 studies; 4,255 biospecimen records encoded
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We used the file ‘sample.tsv’ that contained 4255 rows, each with 39 columns.
findings.study_system: Genomic Data Commons subject/biospecimen metadata; identifier specification

findings.claim: Among acute-febrile-illness research cohorts, fewer than a quarter used an internationally accepted data standard and documented external-access processes were rare, with technical and regulatory issues rated the most important barriers to sharing.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Regarding data standards, less than a quarter of survey respondents (= 18; 23%) reported that the variables collected in their cohort corresponded to an internationally accepted standard.
findings.evidence: International online survey of 78 respondents from 62 AFI cohorts across 23 countries; barriers scored on sliders and classified with the PEARL framework.
findings.effect_size: 23% (18/78) used an international data standard; documented external-access process for 26% clin-epi, 19% samples, 4% genetic data
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Twenty (26%) respondents indicated that their cohort had a documented process for external groups to access clin-epi data, 15 (19%) for human biological samples, and 3 (4%) for human genetic data.
findings.study_system: acute febrile illness research cohorts (62 cohorts, 23 countries) survey

findings.claim: Health researchers overwhelmingly share data privately within their own project team, while public/repository deposition and reuse of others' public data are the least-practiced behaviors.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Results indicate that, on average, participants share their research data with other members in the same research project, with a mean score of 4.74, ranked first among all the statements.
findings.evidence: Questionnaire survey of 362 health scholars measuring data-sharing and reuse behaviors on Likert scales.
findings.effect_size: within-project sharing mean 4.74 (ranked first); 33.1% never reused publicly available data
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The majority of the participants (33.1%) reported never reusing publicly available data.
findings.study_system: health scholars survey, US university

findings.claim: New minimum-information models (MIFE and MIFD) extend the ISA framework to standardize metadata for industrial-biotechnology fermentation experiments and devices, mapping most terms to existing ontologies to ease interoperability and adoption.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In total, 89 terms in MIFE were mapped to existing KOSs such as OM [], PO2 [], and JERM [], among others [,,,,,] (versions from May 2025).
findings.evidence: EU BioIndustry4.0 consortium consensus effort (workshops/webinars over 2 years) producing LinkML/OWL schemas deposited in BioPortal and integrated with FAIR Data Station and FAIRDOM-SEEK.
findings.effect_size: 89 MIFE terms and 26 MIFD terms mapped to existing ontologies
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Similarly to MIFE, 26 terms in MIFD were mapped to existing ontologies (from versions available in May 2025) related to the IB, such as SOSA [], SSN [], and OM [], among others [,], to facilitate interoperability with community standards and effortless adoption by scientists in the field.
findings.study_system: industrial biotechnology fermentation metadata (minimum information model)

findings.claim: Comparing a generic versus a health-domain-specific FAIRification workflow on a diabetes core data set, both achieved the same FAIRness rating with similar resources, implying domain-specific adaptations improve procedural efficiency but not FAIRness scores for core data sets.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Interestingly, the implementation of both workflows led us to achieve the same FAIRness rating and required similar resources for implementation.
findings.evidence: Retrospective implementation of two published FAIRification workflows on the 147-item DZD Core Data Set, assessed with the RDA FAIR Data Maturity Model using 26 of 41 metadata indicators.
findings.effect_size: 26 of 41 FDMM metadata indicators assessed; core data set of 147 data items; 725 views and 379 downloads by Nov 2024
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The FDMM allowed us to discard the data indicators and instead focus on the metadata indicators (26 out of 41 indicators) as is necessary for the FAIR assessment of a CDS.
findings.study_system: German Center for Diabetes Research core data set (FAIRification case study)

findings.claim: A criteria-based systematic review of tabular-health common data models (Sentinel, PCORnet, i2b2, OMOP) and standards found the OMOP/OHDSI network to be the largest observational-data network and FHIR the most widely used interoperability standard.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The OHDSI distributed data network comprises over 331 data sources, containing more than 2.1 billion patient records across 34 countries [].
findings.evidence: Systematic review scoring four CDMs and several data standards against five criteria categories (Suitability, Popularity, Adaptability, Interoperability, Support).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: authors publishing work in journals with mandatory data sharing policies were associated with nearly a tenfold increase in the odds of sharing data than those publishing in journals with no policy (OR: 9.5, 95% CI: 3.26–30.85).
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Even when authors indicate in their manuscript that they will share data upon request, the compliance rate is the same as for authors who do not provide the DAS, suggesting that the DAS may not be sufficient to ensure data sharing.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether journal data-sharing requirements translate into actual availability: a blanket mandatory-deposit policy is associated with ~10x higher odds of sharing, whereas a data-availability statement promising sharing on request yields the same (near-zero) compliance as no statement at all.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The result is an expanding family of ontologies designed to be interoperable and logically well formed and to incorporate accurate representations of biological reality.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Based on our analysis, we estimate that 64% of the UniProtKB proteins are incompletely annotated, and that inconsistent annotations affect 83% of the protein functions and at least 23% of the proteins.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Ontology developers assert coordinated ontologies deliver interoperable, accurate representations enabling data integration, but audits of the resulting Gene Ontology annotations find most protein annotations incomplete and inconsistent, undercutting the reliable-integration promise in practice.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The effectiveness of mandatory data sharing policies varied substantially by journal and type of data, a finding that might be informative for policy makers when designing policies and allocating resources to audit compliance.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Overall, we argue that universal open raw data mandates cannot adequately represent the diversity of qualitative research, and that MIRD may harm rigorous and ethical research practice within health psychology and beyond.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether open-data mandates should be universal: meta-research on (mostly quantitative) medical data treats mandates as effective levers worth strengthening and auditing, while a qualitative-research critique argues universal raw-data mandates are epistemologically and ethically inappropriate and can harm research quality.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The guidelines have been developed with input from a broad spectrum of stakeholders in the proteomics field to represent a true consensus view of the most important data types and metadata, required for a quantitative experiment to be analyzed critically or a data analysis pipeline to be reproduced.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: These shortcomings yielded large discrepancies in the analysis results (e.g., 13,068 vs. 4,923 proteins; 108 vs. 11 differentially expressed proteins), and, in one instance, a highlighted protein lacked robust support in the deposited identifications.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: MIAPE/HUPO-PSI reporting guidelines assert they capture the minimum metadata needed for a proteomics dataset to be critically re-analyzed or a pipeline reproduced, yet a 2026 reanalysis of six public PRIDE deposits found missing metadata and proprietary formats produced large reanalysis discrepancies - i.e. the standards are insufficient or unenforced in practice, leaving open-access data as non-reproducible 'data tombs'.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Only 11.5% of studies completely shared all phenotypes, while 37.9% shared less than 40% of the phenotypes.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: The impact of the shared data is evident in a growing number of published reuses, currently totalling more than 150 publications.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether depositing data in public repositories actually yields reuse: a systematic GEO audit finds most omics studies share badly incomplete metadata (only 11.5% fully), which limits secondary use, whereas a repository built on an enforced community standard (OpenNeuro/BIDS) documents substantial realized reuse (>150 publications) - suggesting enforced standards plus curation, not mere open deposition, drive reuse.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The findings indicate that while some groups are comfortable with metadata and are able to design a metadata structure that works effectively, many users are making little attempts to use it, thereby endangering their ability to recover data in the future.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Templates-based metadata is generated in parallel at each level enabling guided submission of experiment metadata.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether providing metadata infrastructure yields reusable metadata: the LabTrove ELN study finds free-form, user-defined metadata is largely under-used and threatens data recovery, whereas pISA-tree argues templated/guided ISA-model capture ensures standardized metadata. The disagreement is on whether tool design (free-form vs enforced templates) determines metadata quality.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: our results show that open data has significantly increased the citations of journal articles.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: We also find that sharing data in an online repository correlates with a smaller yet still positive citation advantage of 4.3% (±.8) on average.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Magnitude of the open-data citation advantage: a synthetic-control study of a Chinese economics journal mandate reports a large increase in article citations, whereas a 122,000-publication analysis finds only a modest 4.3% advantage for depositing data (and none for sharing code).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Moral and altruistic motives encouraged engagement, whereas financial considerations played a minor, context-dependent role.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Willingness to participate varied by incentive: 60.9% expressed willingness to participate when personal benefits were offered, 29.9% were motivated by public interest, and 9.3% declined participation altogether.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Relative weight of personal/material incentives versus altruism in driving willingness to share genomic/biomedical data: a systematic review concludes financial motives are minor and altruism dominates, whereas a national survey finds personal benefit is the single largest driver of willingness (60.9% vs 29.9% for public interest).

evidence_gaps.topic: FAIR data actually increasing reuse of preclinical/animal data
evidence_gaps.what_is_missing: Primary quantitative demonstration that FAIRification or repository deposition measurably increased downstream reuse of preclinical/animal datasets - the benefit is asserted across many descriptor and review papers but rarely measured.
evidence_gaps.why_it_matters: Risk of false consensus: 'FAIR improves reuse' is repeated widely, yet the causal reuse gain (especially for preclinical data waste) is largely unquantified.

evidence_gaps.topic: Secondary use / repositories for long-tail preclinical animal data
evidence_gaps.what_is_missing: Dedicated repositories and reuse studies for heterogeneous preclinical animal data are scarce; direct database searches for preclinical animal data reuse returned essentially no results beyond isolated commons (ODC-SCI, eTRANSAFE).
evidence_gaps.why_it_matters: Preclinical data waste is the review's core concern, but the infrastructure and evidence base for reusing this specific data type is thin compared with clinical/omics data.

evidence_gaps.what_is_missing: Empirical evaluation linking adoption of minimum-information reporting standards to measurable gains in data interpretability, independent verification, or reuse.
evidence_gaps.why_it_matters: Standards are justified by the promise of independent verifiability, but the downstream effect on actual reuse/reproducibility is not directly demonstrated.

evidence_gaps.what_is_missing: PubMed queries combining MIABE/MIAPE with minimum-information terms returned no usable primary records in this frame; these standards were not retrievable via the queries run.
evidence_gaps.why_it_matters: The cluster's coverage of proteomics (MIAPE) and bioactive-entity (MIABE) reporting standards is currently a gap to close in a continuation frame.

strongest_evidence.claim: Actual public availability of research data in medicine is extremely low (~2% actually shared vs ~8% declared) and voluntary/on-request mechanisms do not work, a pattern independently replicated across many specialties and audits.
strongest_evidence.why_strong: Convergent across a 105-study IPD meta-analysis and multiple independent single-field audits (BMJ 4.5%, oncology, gastroenterology, orthopaedics, BioMed Central author-contact study), with quantified effect sizes and consistent direction.

weakest_evidence_cited.claim: Community/consortium data repositories (FaceBase, ImmuneData, ODC-SCI, RGD) successfully deliver FAIR, reusable data.
weakest_evidence_cited.why_weak: These are self-reported single-consortium descriptor papers reporting adoption metrics (user counts, dataset counts) without independent evaluation of whether the data were actually reused or reproduced downstream.
